title: Voiced K-Row (Dakuten) — が ぎ ぐ げ ご

points.shortDescription: The two small strokes that voice a consonant
points.explanation: Welcome to a turning point in hiragana! The dakuten (゛) — two small diagonal strokes written at the top-right of a character — transforms an unvoiced consonant into its voiced equivalent. 'Voiced' means your vocal cords vibrate while you make the sound. For the K-row: か (ka) becomes が (ga), き (ki) becomes ぎ (gi), く (ku) becomes ぐ (gu), け (ke) becomes げ (ge), こ (ko) becomes ご (go). The same principle applies to the S, T, and H rows, which you'll encounter in upcoming chapters. One dakuten, completely new set of sounds.
rules: Dakuten (゛) = two small strokes top-right = voiced version of that consonant.
K becomes G: か→が, き→ぎ, く→ぐ, け→げ, こ→ご.
Voicing means your vocal cords vibrate — put your hand on your throat: 'k' is silent there, 'g' buzzes.
points.flashcardAnswer: dakuten — makes the consonant voiced (K→G, S→Z, T→D, H→B)

points.name: が
points.explanation: The syllable が is the voiced version of か — replace the unvoiced 'k' with a voiced 'g' as in 'garden' or 'gas'. Your vocal cords vibrate for 'g' but not for 'k'. が is one of the most important particles in Japanese: it marks the grammatical subject of a sentence, especially in clauses where something exists, happens spontaneously, or is preferred. The distinction between the topic particle は and the subject particle が is one of the most discussed points in Japanese grammar — both can mean 'as for / regarding', but が tends to highlight or identify the subject.
rules: が = か + dakuten; voiced 'g' replaces unvoiced 'k'.
が is the subject particle, identifying who or what performs or experiences the action.
は marks the topic (what we're talking about); が marks the grammatical subject (who does it).
points.flashcardAnswer: ga — like the 'ga' in 'garden' (voiced version of か)

points.name: ぎ
points.explanation: The syllable ぎ is the voiced version of き — swap the unvoiced 'k' for a voiced 'g' to get a 'gi' sound as in 'give' or 'gift'. Your tongue makes the same back-of-mouth contact as for き, but now your vocal cords buzz. ぎ appears in important vocabulary: ぎんこう (bank), げんき (energetic/healthy), and the suffix ぎ found in words like うでぎ (arm strength)... Actually, ぎ is perhaps most notable in ぎんこう (bank) — a word every traveler to Japan needs within the first week.
rules: ぎ = き + dakuten; voiced 'g' before 'ee' vowel.
ぎんこう (bank) and げんき (healthy/energetic) are essential vocabulary words.
The voiced 'g' feels like it buzzes in your throat — put a hand on your larynx and feel the difference between き (no buzz) and ぎ (buzz).
points.flashcardAnswer: gi — like the 'gi' in 'give' (voiced version of き)

points.name: ぐ
points.explanation: The syllable ぐ is the voiced version of く — voiced 'g' plus the Japanese unrounded 'u' vowel. Think of it as the beginning of 'good' but with the Japanese flat-lip 'u' rather than the English rounded 'oo'. ぐ appears in ぐち (complaint / grumbling), こぐ (to row a boat), and ぐたぐた (limp / groggy — a useful onomatopoeic word). In conversational Japanese, ぐ also appears in onomatopoeia describing heavy, groggy, or soggy sensations — a sign that you're encountering real Japanese sound-symbolism.
rules: ぐ = く + dakuten; voiced 'g' before the flat, unrounded Japanese 'u'.
Keep lips flat — don't round them into a 'goo' shape.
ぐ appears in onomatopoeia like ぐたぐた (limp/groggy) — Japanese is rich in such expressive words.
points.flashcardAnswer: gu — like the 'gu' in 'good' (voiced version of く)

points.name: げ
points.explanation: The syllable げ is the voiced version of け — voiced 'g' before the 'eh' vowel, like 'ge' in 'get' or 'guest'. げ appears in one of the very first vocabulary sets most learners encounter: げんき (healthy / energetic / fine) is the standard response to 'how are you?' — おげんきですか? (Are you well?) → はい、げんきです (Yes, I'm fine). げた (wooden clogs) and かげ (shadow) round out the common げ vocabulary.
rules: げ = け + dakuten; voiced 'g' before 'eh'.
げんき (healthy/energetic) is one of the most essential vocabulary words in Japanese.
かげ (shadow) and げた (wooden clogs) are common words featuring げ.
points.flashcardAnswer: ge — like the 'ge' in 'get' (voiced version of け)

points.name: ご
points.explanation: The syllable ご is the voiced version of こ — voiced 'g' before the 'oh' vowel, simply sounding like English 'go'. ご appears in extremely high-frequency vocabulary: ごはん (cooked rice / a meal — literally 'honorable rice'), しごと (work / job), ごご (afternoon / PM), and the honorific prefix ご- that politely precedes certain nouns (ごかぞく = your family; ごけんこう = your health). The honorific prefix ご is one of the first grammatical patterns you'll notice in polite Japanese.
rules: ご = こ + dakuten; voiced 'g' before 'oh'.
ごはん (rice/meal) and しごと (work) are two of the most essential words in daily Japanese.
The honorific prefix ご- attaches to nouns to make them polite: ごかぞく = 'your (esteemed) family'.
points.flashcardAnswer: go — like the word 'go' (voiced version of こ)

chapterPractice.prompt: What does the dakuten (゛) do to a character?
choices: Makes it voiced (adds vocal cord vibration)
chapterPractice.explanation: The dakuten (゛) voices a consonant — your vocal cords vibrate when producing it. Put your hand on your throat: か (no buzz) vs が (buzz). This same principle applies to the S, T, and H rows too.

chapterPractice.prompt: Which of these is the voiced version of き?
chapterPractice.explanation: ぎ is the voiced version of き. Add dakuten (゛) to き and you get ぎ — the 'k' sound becomes 'g' with vocal cord vibration.
ごはん (gohan) means 'cooked rice' or 'a meal'. ご (go) + は (ha) + ん (n) = gohan. The ご here is the honorific prefix, and はん means 'rice' — so it's literally 'honorable rice'.
げんき (genki) means 'healthy', 'energetic', or 'fine'. It's the essential response to おげんきですか? ('How are you?'). げ (ge) + ん (n) + き (ki) = genki.
